unit.title: Prepare for oxyacetylene/metal arc welding processes

summary: This unit teaches you to get everything ready before a weld is made by oxy-acetylene welding (OAW) or manual metal arc welding (MMAW). You will learn to read the drawing and job sheet, choose the process and consumables, make the work area safe, mark out, cut, bevel and clean the metal, set up and leak test a gas welding set, set up an arc welding machine, and fit up and tack joints so that they stay in line. You will also learn when to preheat, and how to check, record and report before welding starts.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It is about the work that happens **before the first weld**: planning, choosing the process and consumables, preparing the metal, setting up the equipment and fitting up the joint. Most bad welds start with bad preparation: a joint that is dirty, badly bevelled, out of square or set with the wrong gap. Good preparation makes good welding easy.

The unit covers two processes. **Oxy-acetylene welding (OAW)** melts the metal with a flame of oxygen and acetylene and adds a separate filler rod. **Manual metal arc welding (MMAW)**, or stick welding, melts the metal with an electric arc from a flux-coated electrode. You will set up both, but you are not assessed on welding in this unit: you are assessed on getting the job ready, safely and correctly.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training centres, and anyone starting out in a fabrication shop. You will work mostly on mild steel plate and sheet.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawing, weld symbols and job sheet or welding procedure; list the materials, consumables and equipment; plan the order of work.
Choose the process and consumables
Decide between OAW and MMAW for the metal, thickness, position and place; pick the right electrode or filler rod and keep it in good condition.
Make the work area safe
Clear anything that burns, set up screens and ventilation, have the right extinguisher ready, wear the right PPE, and follow hot work permits on site.
Prepare the material
Check the material, mark out, cut, remove burrs, bevel the edges, and clean the joint area to bright metal.
Set up the gas equipment
Check and assemble the cylinders, regulators, flashback arrestors, hoses and torch; leak test every joint; light and set a neutral flame; shut down safely.
Set up the arc equipment
Check the machine, leads, holder and clamp; connect the polarity the electrode needs; set and test the current.
Fit up and tack
Hold the parts with clamps or a jig, set the gap and alignment, pre-set where needed, tack in a sensible order, and check again.
Control distortion and preheat
Use tacking, clamping, pre-setting and a balanced order; preheat when the procedure says, and check the temperature.
Check, record and report
Check the job is ready, write the details on the job card, and tag out and report faulty equipment or wrong materials.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, drawings, choosing the process, cleaning, work area safety, gas and arc set-up, consumables, fit-up, distortion, preheat, PPE and reporting.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms such as root face, regulator, jig and reference line) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: preparing and tacking single-V butt joints and tee joints for MMAW, and assembling, leak testing and lighting an oxy-acetylene set and preparing sheet for gas welding. The assessor watches your safety, your checks and your method, not only the finished joint.

blocks.note: Learn the trade words in the Revision section. Short-answer questions want the exact word: root face, root gap, reference line, regulator, flashback arrestor, jig, fire watch, WPS.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the job from the drawing

blocks.p: Never start cutting until you understand the job. Read the **drawing** and the **job sheet** first, then plan the order of work. Ten minutes of reading saves hours of putting mistakes right.

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: Drawing
The shape and sizes of every part, in millimetres
The joint types and where each weld goes (weld symbols)
The material and thickness, often in the title block or a parts list
Notes such as finish, tolerances and scale
Job sheet or job card
The job number, the customer and the date it is needed
The process to use and the materials to draw from the store
Space to record what you used and the checks you made
Welding procedure specification (WPS)
The tested method for the weld: process, joint preparation, filler or electrode, size, current or nozzle, position
Any preheat, and how to check it
Used on important work; if there is one, follow it exactly
Maker's instructions and charts
Electrode packet: current range and polarity
Nozzle chart: nozzle size and gas pressures for the thickness
Machine and equipment manuals

blocks.note: **WPS** stands for welding procedure specification. It is written and tested before production starts, so that every welder who follows it gets a sound weld. You do not change it on your own: if something on it cannot be done, ask your instructor or supervisor.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Read the drawing, job sheet and any WPS; ask about anything unclear
List the materials, consumables, tools and equipment; check that they are in the store
Check and prepare the work area and your PPE
Mark out and cut the parts; remove burrs
Prepare the edges (bevel) and clean the joint areas
Set up and check the welding equipment
Fit up, tack and check the joints; preheat if the procedure says
Record the details on the job card; have the set-up checked before welding

blocks.p: A weld symbol tells the welder what weld to make and where. It is built on an **arrow** and a horizontal **reference line**. The arrow points to the joint. Everything else is written on or around the reference line.

head: Part of the symbol
What it means
rows: Arrow
Points to the joint to be welded. The side of the joint the arrow touches is the **arrow side**; the far side is the **other side**.
Reference line
The horizontal line the arrow joins. The weld symbol, sizes and other signs sit on it.
Triangle
A fillet weld
V shape
A single-V butt weld (both edges bevelled)
Two short upright lines
A square-edge butt weld (no bevel)
Half a V (one upright line and one slanted line)
A single-bevel butt weld: only one edge is bevelled, as on a tee butt joint
Number to the left of the symbol
The size of the weld, for example the leg length of a fillet. ISO drawings put a letter in front: **z6** means a 6 mm leg length; **a4** means a 4 mm throat thickness.
Numbers to the right of the symbol
The length of the weld, and the spacing if it is a broken (intermittent) weld. No number means weld the full length.
Small circle where the arrow meets the line
Weld all round the joint
Small flag where the arrow meets the line
A site (field) weld: made on site, not in the workshop
Tail (a fork at the far end of the line)
Extra information, such as the process or the WPS number. ISO process numbers: **111** = MMAW; **311** = oxy-acetylene welding.
Straight or curved line over the symbol
The shape of the weld face: flat (flush) or convex

blocks.p: There are two systems in use, and Jamaican shops see drawings in both, so check which one your drawing uses.

head: System
Weld on the arrow side
Weld on the other side
rows: American (AWS)
Symbol **below** the reference line
Symbol **above** the reference line
ISO (international)
Symbol on the **solid** reference line
Symbol on the **dashed** line drawn beside the solid line

blocks.p: A symbol on both sides of the line means weld both sides, for example a double fillet on a tee joint.

blocks.note: Measure, do not guess. Check the plate thickness with a steel rule or, better, a vernier caliper, and check the lengths with a rule or tape. Check that the material is what the drawing names (for example mild steel, not galvanised). If it is wrong, do not use it: report it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Both OAW and MMAW can weld mild steel, but each is better for some jobs. The drawing or WPS may name the process. When it does not, your instructor or supervisor will decide with you, using the points below.

head: Point
Oxy-acetylene welding (OAW)
Manual metal arc welding (MMAW)
rows: Heat source
Flame of oxygen and acetylene, about 3 100 °C at the tip of the inner cone
Electric arc between a flux-coated electrode and the work, several thousand degrees and very concentrated
Filler metal
A separate filler rod fed into the pool by hand
The electrode's core wire melts and becomes the filler
Protection of the weld
The flame's outer envelope keeps air away
The flux makes a gas shield and a slag cover
Heat input
Soft, spread out and easy to control; heats a wide area
Concentrated and fast; heats a narrow band
Best for
Thin sheet (up to about 3 mm)
Small-bore pipe and tube
Repairs and small jobs
The same set can braze, heat, bend and cut
Plate about 3 mm and thicker
Structural steel, gates, frames, trailers
Site and outdoor work
Most positions with the right electrode
Weak points
Slow on thick plate
Wide heat gives more distortion
Cylinders to move, store and look after
Burns through thin sheet easily
Needs a power supply or an engine-driven welder
Arc rays, slag and spatter

ul: **Thickness:** thin sheet favours OAW; plate of about 3 mm and up favours MMAW.
**Material:** both suit mild steel; some metals need another process. Check the drawing.
**Strength needed:** load-bearing and structural welds are usually made by MMAW (or another arc process) to a WPS.
**Position and access:** a small torch reaches tight places; MMAW works in all positions with the right electrode.
**Where the job is:** with no mains power on a farm or site, an engine-driven arc welder or a gas set may be the only choice.
**What the drawing or WPS says:** this comes first. If it names a process, use it.

blocks.p: Choose the electrode the drawing or WPS gives. For general mild steel work the usual choice is a rutile electrode such as **E6013**; where welds carry heavy loads or must resist cracking, a low-hydrogen electrode such as **E7018** is used. The size is the diameter of the core wire: thicker plate needs a bigger electrode and more current. The packet gives the current range and the polarity.

head: Plate thickness (guide)
Typical electrode size
rows: About 1.5–3 mm
About 3–6 mm
About 6–10 mm
About 10 mm and up
4.0 mm and up (root runs often with a smaller size)

blocks.note: These are guide figures only. Follow the drawing or WPS, the packet, and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: For mild steel, use **copper-coated mild steel filler rod**. The thin copper coat stops the rod rusting in storage; it does not change the weld.
Choose the rod size from the job sheet or chart: thin sheet needs a thin rod (for 1.6 mm sheet, often a 1.6 mm rod).
Mild steel gas welding needs no flux. Brazing, and welding some other metals, do need one.
Rods must be clean, dry and free of rust, oil and paint: dirt on the rod goes into the weld pool and causes porosity and weak welds.
Keep rods in labelled tubes or racks, sorted by type and size. A rod you cannot identify must not be used.

head: Consumable
How to store it
Why
rows: Rutile electrodes (E6013)
In their packets, in a dry store off the floor
Out of the rain and away from doors and windows
Damp flux gives porosity, spatter and a poor arc
Low-hydrogen electrodes (E7018)
Sealed until needed
Once opened, in a heated electrode oven at the maker's temperature (often about 120–150 °C)
Damp ones re-baked as the packet says
Moisture puts hydrogen into the weld, which causes porosity and cracking
Gas filler rods
In labelled tubes or racks, dry
Kept away from oil and grease
Rust and dirt spoil the weld
Gas cylinders
Upright and chained, in a shaded, ventilated area away from heat
Oxygen kept apart from fuel gas
Valves closed and caps on when not in use
Full and empty cylinders kept separate
A heated cylinder can leak or burst; oxygen makes any fire much fiercer

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, especially in the rainy seasons, gets into opened electrode packets within days. Take out only what you will use soon, close the packet, and put unused electrodes back. Never leave electrodes on a bench overnight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Handle electrodes and rods with clean, dry gloves.
Do not drop or bend electrodes: the flux can crack and fall off.
Use the oldest stock first (first in, first out), so packets do not sit until they spoil.
Hand in electrodes with cracked or crumbling flux, rusty ends or a damp packet, and rods that are rusty or unlabelled.

sections.title: A safe work area and the right PPE

blocks.p: Preparing for welding brings its own hazards: grinding sparks and discs, fuel gas and oxygen, fumes from coatings and cleaners, heavy and sharp plate, and later the arc or flame itself. Make the area safe **before** you start, not after something goes wrong.

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
How you control it
rows: Fire
Sparks from grinding, cutting and welding can fly 10 metres or more and smoulder in rags, wood, dust or rubbish
Clear or cover anything that burns
Check for gaps in floors and walls
Extinguisher of the right type at hand
Fire watch during and after the work
Explosion
Leaking fuel gas; drums or tanks that held fuel; oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Leak test the gas set
Never weld or cut a container that held fuel unless a competent person has made it safe
Keep oxygen fittings clean and oil-free
Fumes and gases
Coatings (paint, zinc, oil), cleaning solvents, and the welding itself
Clean coatings off the weld area
Ventilation or extraction near the work
Respirator when your instructor says
Arc radiation
The MMAW arc gives off UV and IR rays that burn eyes and skin
Screens round the bay
Warn people before striking
Correct filter shade
Flying particles and noise
Grinding, chipping and wire brushing
Safety glasses and a face shield
Ear protection
Cuts and crushing
Sharp edges and burrs, heavy plate
Leather gloves
Safety boots
Safe lifting; get help
Electric shock
Damaged leads, wet conditions
Check the equipment
Keep dry
Switch off before changing connections

blocks.h: Making the area safe for hot work

flow: Look round about 10 metres, including above and below the work
Move away anything that burns (paper, rags, wood, oil, paint, dry grass); cover what cannot be moved with a fire blanket
Check that sparks cannot fall through gaps in the floor, walls or decking
Put a suitable extinguisher (for example dry powder or carbon dioxide) within reach, and know how to use it
Put up welding screens and warn people nearby
Switch on extraction or check that air moves through the area
Check the floor is dry and clear, with cables and hoses laid out of the way and a clear way out
Check gas cylinders are upright, chained and away from the hot work

blocks.h: Hot work permits and fire watch

blocks.p: A **hot work permit** is written permission to weld, cut or grind in a place outside the normal workshop, such as a factory, hotel, school or building site. An authorised person (for example the site's maintenance manager) issues it only after the area has been checked. It says where and when the work may be done, the precautions to take, and who keeps the fire watch. You must follow every condition on it, and hand it back when the job is finished.

A **fire watch** is a person who watches the area for smoke, smouldering or fire while the work goes on and for a set time afterwards, with an extinguisher ready. Many workplaces ask for at least 30 minutes after the last hot work, and some for an hour or more: follow the permit.

ul: Use the degreaser your instructor gives you, on a cloth, in a ventilated place, away from sparks and flames.
**Never use chlorinated solvents** (some degreasers and brake cleaners) near arc welding: the arc's UV light turns their vapour into **phosgene**, a poisonous gas. Read the label.
Let cleaned metal dry fully, and let the vapour clear, before any welding or cutting starts: solvent vapour can catch fire.
Keep solvent tins closed, labelled and stored away from the welding area.

blocks.p: Heating zinc (galvanising) gives off fumes that cause **metal fume fever**: flu-like chills, fever, aches and sickness some hours later. Paint, plastic coatings and oil also give off harmful fumes. Grind or wire-brush the coating off the weld area, use extraction, and wear the respirator your instructor gives you.

head: Task
PPE you need
rows: Grinding bevels and cleaning with a power brush
Safety glasses with a **face shield** over them
Leather gloves
Ear plugs or muffs
Cotton overalls or flame-resistant clothing, safety boots
Cutting with an abrasive saw or cutting torch
Safety glasses and face shield (or cutting goggles for the torch)
Gloves, ear protection, flame-resistant clothing, boots
Oxy-acetylene welding
Gas welding goggles or face shield with a tinted filter (often shade 4 to 6 for steel; follow the chart)
Leather gloves, flame-resistant clothing, boots
MMAW and tacking
Welding helmet with the right filter (often shade 10 to 13), clear safety glasses underneath
Leather gauntlet gloves, flame-resistant clothing with sleeves down and collar closed, leather apron or sleeves when needed, safety boots

blocks.note: Gas welding goggles (shade 4 to 6) do **not** protect your eyes from an electric arc. Never tack with MMAW while wearing gas goggles.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check your gloves before you start: holes let in heat and sparks, and damp gloves let current through.
Wear cotton or wool, not nylon or polyester: synthetic cloth melts onto the skin.
Take lighters and matches out of your pockets.
Plate is heavy and its edges are sharp. Wear gloves and safety boots.
Plan the lift: check the weight, clear the route and the place where the plate will go.
Bend your knees, keep your back straight, hold the load close and do not twist. Get help or use a trolley, hoist or plate clamp for heavy plate.
Never drag a plate by one corner or carry a long length alone.
Keep the floor clear of offcuts, tools, cables and hoses: trips near hot work and sharp edges cause serious injuries.
Put offcuts in the scrap bin and tools back in their places; lost tools waste time.
Keep extinguishers, fire exits and isolating switches clear and easy to reach.
Check the type and thickness against the drawing: measure the thickness with a vernier caliper or a rule.
Check the size of the sheet or plate, and that it is flat and not badly pitted, cracked or laminated (split in layers along its edge).
Look for the grade or batch markings, and record them on the job card if your workplace asks you to.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Steel rule and tape
Measuring lengths and positions
Engineer's square (try square)
Marking and checking lines and edges at 90°
Scriber
Scratching a fine, accurate line on clean steel
Soapstone or a paint marker
Lines that must show up through heat and dirt, for example on cutting lines and on plate for welding
Centre punch
A small dot to mark the centre of a hole or the ends of a line
Bevel gauge or protractor
Setting and checking bevel angles
Dividers
Marking arcs and circles, and stepping off equal spacings

blocks.note: Mark out from a straight, square edge (a datum edge), and measure every part from it, so errors do not add up. Check your marking against the drawing before you cut.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Cut on the **waste side** of the line, so the part ends up the right size.
Use the right method: guillotine or snips for sheet; hacksaw, bandsaw or abrasive cut-off saw for bar and section; oxy-fuel or plasma cutting for thicker plate and shapes.
Remove the **burrs** (sharp, rough edges left by cutting) with a file or grinder. Burrs cut hands and stop the parts fitting closely.
Flame-cut edges have a hard oxide layer and sometimes slag: grind them back to clean metal before welding.

blocks.p: Thin metal can be welded with square edges, because the heat goes right through. Thicker plate is **bevelled** so the arc or flame can reach the bottom of the joint, the **root**, and the weld can go right through the joint.

head: Preparation
Typical use
Typical sizes (always follow the drawing or WPS)
rows: Square edge (close or with a small gap)
OAW on sheet; MMAW on plate up to about 3 mm
Gap as the job sheet gives; edges straight and clean
Flanged edge
Very thin sheet (about 1 mm and less) for OAW
Edges turned up and melted down without filler
Single-V
MMAW on plate from about 6 mm, welded from one side
Included angle about **60°** (about 30° on each plate)
Root face about 1–2 mm (some procedures give up to 3 mm)
Root gap about 2–3 mm
Single bevel
Tee butt joints and corner joints where one plate is bevelled
Bevel about 45° on one plate
Double-V
Thick plate welded from both sides
Less weld metal and less distortion than a single-V on the same plate

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Bevel
The sloping edge ground or cut on a plate
Bevel angle
The angle of the slope on one plate
Included angle
The total angle between the two bevels: two 30° bevels make a 60° included angle
Root face (land)
The small flat left at the bottom of the bevel; it stops the root burning away
Root gap
The space between the plate edges at the root; it lets the root run penetrate through

head: Mistake
What it does to the weld
rows: Root face too thick
The root run cannot melt through: **incomplete root penetration**
Root face too thin or ground to a knife edge
The root burns away and sags through: **burn-through** and excess penetration
Root gap too small or closed up
Poor penetration at the root
Root gap too wide
Burn-through, and the joint is hard to bridge
Uneven root face or gap along the joint
Penetration that comes and goes along the weld
Included angle too wide
More weld metal, more time, more heat and **more distortion**
Included angle too narrow
The electrode cannot reach the root; lack of fusion on the sides and trapped slag

blocks.h: How to bevel with an angle grinder

flow: Check the grinder, the disc (right type, not cracked, rated for the grinder's speed) and the guard; put on glasses, face shield, gloves and ear protection
Mark the bevel line on the face of the plate and the root face line on its edge
Clamp the plate firmly so it cannot move
Grind the bevel with a grinding disc, holding the grinder with both hands and keeping the angle steady
Leave the root face; file or grind it flat and even along the whole edge
Check the angle with a bevel gauge or protractor, and the root face with a rule
Finish with a flap disc and remove the burrs

blocks.note: Point the sparks away from people, gas cylinders and anything that burns. Unplug the grinder before changing the disc. Never use a cutting disc for heavy side grinding: it can shatter.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Rust, **mill scale** (the blue-black skin on hot-rolled steel), paint, oil, grease and moisture spoil a weld. They cause porosity, slag inclusions and lack of fusion. Clean the joint faces and a band on each side (about 25 mm, or as the procedure says) to bright metal.

head: Method
Use
rows: Wire brush (hand or power)
Loose rust, slag and dirt
Grinding disc or flap disc
Mill scale, heavy rust, paint and galvanising
Emery cloth
Thin sheet and filler rods for gas welding, where a grinder would remove too much metal
Degreaser on a cloth
Oil and grease; then let it dry fully

blocks.note: In Jamaica's humid air, bright steel can start to rust overnight. Clean the joint as close as you can to the time you weld it, and keep cleaned parts dry and under cover.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An oxy-acetylene set holds two gases under pressure: **oxygen**, which makes anything burn much more fiercely, and **acetylene**, a fuel gas that is very easy to set alight. Set it up carefully, in the right order, with clean hands and tools, and test every joint for leaks before you light it.

blocks.h: The parts, in order from cylinder to torch

flow: Cylinder and cylinder valve
Regulator
Flashback arrestor
Hose
Non-return valve
Torch (blowpipe) and nozzle

head: Part
Its job
What to check
rows: Oxygen cylinder
Holds oxygen at very high pressure (often about 150–200 bar when full)
Label shows oxygen (do not rely on colour alone)
Chained upright on the trolley
Valve outlet clean, undamaged and free of oil and grease
Acetylene cylinder
Holds acetylene dissolved in acetone in a porous filling, at a much lower pressure
Label shows acetylene
**Upright** and chained
Valve outlet clean and undamaged; valve key to hand
Regulator
Lowers the high cylinder pressure to a steady low working pressure; one gauge shows the cylinder contents, the other the working pressure
Right regulator for the gas
Gauges not cracked and needles at zero
Threads and seal undamaged
Adjusting screw wound out (loose)
Flashback arrestor
Fitted at each regulator outlet; stops a flame burning back into the regulator and cylinder, and stops gas flowing the wrong way
Fitted on both gases
Right way round (arrow towards the torch)
Within its test or replacement date
Hoses
Carry the gases to the torch; **red for fuel gas**, blue (or green on American-style sets) for oxygen
No cracks, cuts, burns, kinks or worn spots along the whole length
Clips or crimped ends tight
No home-made joints
Non-return valves
Fitted at the torch inlets; let gas flow only towards the torch
Fitted on both inlets
Torch (blowpipe) and nozzle
Mixes the gases and burns them at the nozzle; the valves on the torch control the flame
Valves close fully
Nozzle the right size from the maker's chart, clean and undamaged

ul: **Oxygen** fittings have **right-hand** threads (tighten clockwise).
**Fuel gas** fittings have **left-hand** threads (tighten anticlockwise). Their nuts usually have a notch or groove cut round them so you can tell them apart.
Different threads mean an oxygen regulator cannot be fitted to a fuel gas cylinder by mistake. Never force a fitting or change an adaptor to make it fit.
Tighten fittings with the correct spanner, firmly but not with great force. Never use grease, oil, jointing compound or tape on gas fittings.

blocks.note: **Oil and grease near oxygen** can catch fire or explode on their own when oxygen under pressure reaches them. Keep oxygen fittings, regulators and your hands and gloves free of oil and grease. Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or to cool yourself: clothing soaked with oxygen bursts into flame from a single spark.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Check that the cylinders are the right gases, upright and chained on the trolley; if the acetylene cylinder has been lying down, stand it upright and leave it for the time the gas supplier gives before use
Wipe each valve outlet with a clean, dry, lint-free cloth; check for damage and oil
Check each regulator, wind out its adjusting screw, and fit it to the right cylinder
Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet
Check the hoses along their whole length and connect them: red to the fuel gas, blue or green to the oxygen
Fit the non-return valves and the torch; choose the nozzle from the maker's chart for the thickness and fit it
Make sure the torch valves are closed

blocks.note: Some gas suppliers tell you to 'crack' a cylinder valve (open it briefly) to blow out dust before fitting the regulator; others forbid it, especially on fuel gas. Follow your gas supplier's and the Centre's rules.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Opening the cylinders and setting the pressures

ul: Stand to the side of the regulator, never in front of its gauges, and open each cylinder valve **slowly**.
Open the acetylene valve no more than about one and a half turns, and leave the key on the valve so it can be shut quickly in an emergency.
Set the working pressures given on the nozzle chart by turning the regulator's adjusting screw in.
**Never use acetylene above about 1 bar (15 psi).** Above this pressure acetylene can break down violently and explode, even with no air or flame present.
Never use copper pipe or fittings of pure copper with acetylene: they form an explosive compound. (Brass fittings made for acetylene are safe.)

flow: With the cylinder valves open and the pressures set (torch valves closed), brush leak-detection solution or soapy water on every joint
Check the cylinder valve spindle and outlet, the regulator inlet and outlet, the arrestors, both ends of each hose and the torch connections
Watch for bubbles: a growing bubble means a leak
If there is a leak: shut the cylinder valves, release the pressure, tighten or replace the part, then test again
Never look for a leak with a flame

blocks.note: Use leak-detection fluid made for gas equipment, or plain soap and water with no oil in it: oily soap on oxygen fittings is a fire risk.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Purging, lighting and setting a neutral flame

flow: Purge each hose on its own: open one torch valve for a few seconds to clear out air or mixed gas, then close it; do this away from any flame
Point the torch away from people, cylinders and anything that burns
Open the fuel gas valve a little and light the gas with a **spark lighter** (never a match or cigarette lighter)
Turn up the fuel gas until the flame stops making black smoke and soot
Open the oxygen valve slowly: a white feather appears round a bright inner cone
Keep adding oxygen until the feather just disappears into the inner cone: this is a **neutral flame**

head: Flame
How it looks
Use
rows: Carburising (reducing)
Too much acetylene: a white feather round the inner cone
A few special jobs such as hard-facing; not for welding mild steel
Neutral
Equal gases: a clear, rounded inner cone with no feather
Welding mild steel
Oxidising
Too much oxygen: a short, pointed inner cone and a harsh hissing sound
Some brazing and bronze welding; it burns mild steel and leaves a sparky, porous weld

ul: A **backfire** is a sharp pop when the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle, often because the nozzle is blocked, overheated or touching the work. Shut the torch valves, find the cause, clean or cool the nozzle, then relight.

A **flashback** is the flame burning back inside the torch or hoses, with a squeal or hiss and a hot torch. Close the torch oxygen valve, then the fuel gas valve, then both cylinder valves. Do not use the set again until it has been checked, and report it.

flow: Close the torch valves to put out the flame (most centres close the fuel gas first, then the oxygen: follow your Centre's rule)
Close both cylinder valves
Open each torch valve in turn to bleed the gas out of its hose, until both gauges read zero, then close it
Wind out both regulator adjusting screws
Coil the hoses without kinks and hang them up; leave the area tidy

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun can make a cylinder very hot. Keep cylinders in the shade, never beside a furnace, a forge or hot work, and never where a welding arc or flame can touch them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An arc welding machine changes mains power into a high current at a low voltage. Before you switch it on, check it, connect it correctly, and set the current for the electrode you will use. A loose lead or a cracked holder can give a shock, start a fire or ruin the weld.

ul: On a dry, level floor, out of the rain, out of direct sun and away from puddles.
With space round it so the fan can draw cooling air through the vents; never covered or boxed in.
Connected to the supply its rating plate asks for. Jamaica's supply is 110 V or 220 V at 50 Hz; most welding machines need a 220 V outlet on a circuit able to carry their current.
Only a qualified electrician connects, repairs or changes mains plugs, sockets and wiring.

head: Item
Check
rows: Mains plug and cable
No cuts, burns, loose plug or bare wires
Machine case
Closed, undamaged, vents clear; any DO NOT USE tag?
Welding leads
Insulation not cut, burnt or worn through; thick enough for the current; not longer than needed
Connections
Lead connectors pushed in and twisted tight in the machine terminals; tight at the holder and clamp. **A loose connection overheats and makes the arc unsteady.**
Electrode holder
Insulation whole, not cracked or burnt; jaws clean and gripping firmly
Work return clamp
Spring firm, jaws clean; it will be fixed to clean metal on the job or the welding bench, close to the weld, never to the machine case

blocks.p: On a DC machine the electrode lead can go to the positive (+) or the negative (−) terminal. The electrode packet tells you which. On AC the current changes direction 100 times a second on Jamaica's 50 Hz supply, so polarity does not apply.

head: Name
Stands for
Electrode lead to
Work return lead to
rows: DCEP (DC+)
Direct current electrode positive
+ (positive)
− (negative)
DCEN (DC−)
Direct current electrode negative
− (negative)
+ (positive)

blocks.note: Always switch the machine off before you change the leads over or alter any connection.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Welding current is measured in **amps (A)**.
Find the current range for the electrode type and size on the **packet or data sheet**, and set it near the middle of that range.
Run a short test bead on scrap of the same thickness, then adjust in small steps. Too low: the electrode sticks and the bead sits on top. Too high: lots of spatter, a red-hot electrode and undercut.
Thicker plate and fillet welds need a little more current; vertical and overhead work a little less.

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** on the rating plate shows how many minutes in every 10 the machine can weld at a given current without overheating, for example 150 A at 60% means 6 minutes in every 10. In a hot Jamaican workshop a machine can overheat sooner, so keep it shaded with its vents clear.

flow: Screens up and people warned
Helmet with the right filter, safety glasses, gloves and full clothing
Machine checked, leads connected for the right polarity
Work clamp on clean metal near the joint
Current set from the packet and tested on scrap
Electrode dry and undamaged

blocks.p: **Fit-up** is putting the parts together in the right position, with the right gap, square and in line, ready for welding. **Tack welds** then hold them there. A good fit-up gives an even weld; a poor one gives uneven penetration, distortion and a job that does not match the drawing.

head: Tool
Use
rows: Engineer's square
Checking that parts are at 90° (for example the upright of a tee joint), from both sides
Steel rule and tape
Checking positions, lengths and diagonals
Spacer wire or gap gauge
Setting an even root gap: a piece of wire or rod of the right diameter held in the gap while tacking
G-clamps, toggle clamps and vice-grip clamps
Holding parts in place on the bench
Welding magnets
Holding plates at 90° or 45° while tacking
Jig or fixture
A frame or holder that keeps parts in the right place for tacking and welding; it makes repeat parts the same
Straightedge
Checking that butt-jointed plates are in line, with no step (misalignment) between them

blocks.h: Fitting up a single-V butt joint

flow: Lay the bevelled plates on a flat bench, bevels facing each other
Set the root gap evenly along the joint with a spacer wire
Check that the plates are level with each other: no step (high-low) at the root
Set the pre-set angle if the job sheet asks for it (see Distortion below)
Tack at each end on the root side, check the gap again, then add tacks along a longer joint
Remove the spacer, clean the slag off the tacks, and check the gap, alignment and pre-set once more
Clean both plates where the weld goes, and mark a line on the base plate where the upright stands
Stand the upright on the line and hold it with a clamp or welding magnet
Check it at 90° with an engineer's square from both sides
Check that the joint is tight along its length, or has the small even gap the drawing gives
Tack one end, check square again, then tack the other end; add tacks along a longer joint
Check again after tacking; correct the joint before welding if it has moved

ul: **Small but well fused**, so the main weld can melt them in. A tack that is only stuck on can crack or leave lack of fusion.
Long enough to hold (often about 10–15 mm on plate; shorter on thin sheet) and placed so the welder can weld over them.
Closer together on thin sheet than on thick plate, because thin sheet moves more with heat.
Made with the same care, electrode or rod as the main weld, after the same cleaning.
Chipped and brushed clean before welding over them.
If a joint moves out of line after tacking, grind or break the tack, re-set the parts and tack again. Do not weld it as it is and hope to straighten it later.

blocks.p: Steel expands when it is heated and shrinks as it cools. The weld and the metal next to it are heated most, so they shrink most as they cool, and they pull the parts with them. A butt joint welded from one side bends up towards the weld; the upright of a tee joint welded on one side pulls over towards the weld; a frame welded one joint at a time pulls out of square. This is **distortion**.

head: Method
How it controls distortion
rows: Accurate parts and edge preparation
A good fit and the right bevel need less weld metal, so there is less shrinkage
Clamps, jigs and fixtures
Hold the parts firmly while the weld cools
Balanced tacking
Tacks at each end, then the middle, or on opposite sides in turn, so the pulls cancel
Pre-setting
Setting the parts slightly out of line the opposite way (often a few degrees) so the weld pulls them straight as it shrinks
Balanced welding order
Welding opposite sides or joints in turn, and short runs in a planned order (back-stepping)
Not over-welding
The right weld size only: extra weld metal means extra shrinkage

blocks.note: Pre-set the upright of a tee joint that will be welded on one side only by leaning it a little **away** from the weld side. The weld then pulls it back to 90° as it cools. Check with your square after welding to learn how much pre-set your joints need.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Preheat** means warming the parts before welding. It slows the cooling of the weld and the metal beside it. Fast cooling can make some steels hard and brittle near the weld, and they can crack. Preheat also drives off moisture.

ul: **When:** when the WPS or your instructor says. Usually for thick sections, medium- and high-carbon steels, cast iron, and parts that are cold and damp.

**How:** with a heating torch, heating a wide band on both sides of the joint evenly, not just one spot. The WPS gives the temperature and often where to check it (for example a set distance from the joint).
**How to check:** a **temperature-indicating crayon** or a contact thermometer. Never judge by touch or by colour.

head: Crayon mark on the steel
What it tells you
rows: The mark melts and goes liquid and glossy within a second or two
The steel has reached (or passed) the crayon's temperature
The mark stays dry and chalky
The steel is still below that temperature: keep heating

blocks.note: Choose the crayon rated for the temperature in the WPS. A crayon rated at 150 °C tells you only whether the steel is above or below 150 °C. To check that a part is not too hot, use a second crayon rated at the upper limit.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Check
Ready when
rows: Drawing and job sheet
Read and understood; any questions answered
Material
Right type and thickness, marked out and cut to size, deburred
Joints
Edges prepared to the right angle and root face; cleaned to bright metal; fitted with the right gap, square or pre-set; tacked and cleaned
Consumables
Right electrode or rod, dry and undamaged
Equipment
Checked, connected correctly, leak tested (gas) or test-run on scrap (arc)
Area and PPE
Burnables cleared, extinguisher ready, screens up, ventilation on, full PPE
Preheat
Done and checked, if the procedure asks for it

blocks.h: Faulty equipment: stop, tag and report

flow: Stop: do not use the faulty item
Make it safe: switch off and unplug it, or close the gas
Put a **DO NOT USE** tag on it with the fault, the date and your name
Tell your instructor or supervisor at once
Write it in the fault book or on the job card

head: Fault you might find
What it could cause
rows: Cracked regulator body or gauge
Gas escaping; a regulator bursting under cylinder pressure
Hose with a burn, cut or crack
A gas leak and fire at the hose
Oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Fire or explosion when oxygen flows
Missing flashback arrestor
A flashback reaching the regulator or cylinder
Cut or burnt welding lead, cracked holder
Electric shock, arcing and fire
Grinder guard missing or disc cracked
A disc bursting and hitting you

blocks.p: A **DO NOT USE** tag means the item is faulty and nobody may use it until it has been repaired and checked. Never remove someone else's tag.

ul: If the plate, electrodes or filler rods are not what the drawing or job sheet asks for (wrong thickness, grade, type or size), do not use them.
Set them aside, label them, and tell your instructor or supervisor.
Never 'make do' with a thinner plate or a different electrode: a weld that looks fine can fail in use.

blocks.p: The job card records what was used and done, so that the job can be **traced and checked later**. If a weld ever fails, the record shows which material, consumables and settings were used and who did the work.

ul: Job number and drawing number
Material type, thickness, and any batch or heat number
Process, and electrode or filler rod type, size and batch
Settings: current and polarity, or nozzle size and pressures
Preheat temperature, if used
Checks made, faults found and reported
Your name and the date

blocks.note: Reporting is not getting someone into trouble. A cracked regulator reported today is a fire prevented tomorrow.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing and job sheet, and say what a WPS is for.
I can read the parts of a weld symbol, including the arrow side and other side, size, weld-all-round, site weld and tail.
I can plan the order of work for a welding job.
I can compare OAW and MMAW and choose the better process for a job.
I can choose electrodes and filler rods, and store and handle them so they stay clean and dry.
I can make a work area safe for hot work, and explain a hot work permit and a fire watch.
I can choose the right PPE for grinding, gas welding and arc welding.
I can check material, mark out, cut and deburr it.
I can bevel plate for a single-V butt joint with the right angle and root face, and explain what goes wrong if they are wrong.
I can clean a joint area to bright metal and use cleaning chemicals safely.
I can check and assemble an oxy-acetylene set, leak test it, light a neutral flame and shut it down.
I can explain why acetylene is kept below 1 bar and why oil must be kept away from oxygen.
I can check and set up an MMAW machine, connect the polarity from the packet and set the current.
I can fit up and tack butt and tee joints with the right gap, square and in line.
I can explain why distortion happens and how to control it while preparing a job.
I can say when and why preheat is used, and check it with a temperature crayon.
I can tag out and report faulty equipment and wrong materials, and fill in a job card.

terms: A sharp pop as the flame goes out or snaps back into the nozzle
A sloping edge cut or ground on a plate so the weld can reach the root
A sharp, rough edge left by cutting
A gas flame with too much acetylene, shown by a white feather
Direct current electrode positive: the electrode lead goes to the + terminal
Parts pulled out of shape or line by the weld shrinking as it cools
How many minutes in every 10 a machine can weld at a given current
A person watching a hot work area for fire during and after the work
Putting the parts together in position, with the right gap and alignment, ready to tack
The flame burning back inside the torch or hoses
A safety device at the regulator outlet that stops a flashback reaching the regulator and cylinder
Written permission to weld, cut or grind in a place, given after safety checks
The total angle between the two bevels of a V joint
A frame or holder that keeps parts in the right place for tacking and welding; also called a fixture
The blue-black skin on hot-rolled steel
A gas flame with balanced oxygen and acetylene: a clear inner cone and no feather
A valve at the torch inlet that lets gas flow only towards the torch
A gas flame with too much oxygen: a short, pointed cone and a hiss
Warming the parts before welding to slow cooling and prevent cracking
Setting parts slightly out of line so the weld's shrinkage pulls them straight
Letting a little gas flow through each hose to clear out air or mixed gas before lighting
The horizontal line of a weld symbol that the arrow joins
The device that lowers cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
The bottom of the joint, which the weld must reach
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevel; also called the land
The space between the plate edges at the root
A hardened, pointed tool for scratching lines on metal
A short weld that holds the parts in place before the main weld
A crayon that melts at a set temperature, used to check preheat
Welding procedure specification: the tested method and settings for a weld

c1.title: A trailer drawbar in Old Harbour
c1.text: Odane, a Level 2 trainee on work placement at a fabrication shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine, is preparing two pieces of 12 mm mild steel plate for a single-V butt joint on a farm-trailer drawbar. The drawing uses the American (AWS) weld symbol system. The symbol has a V below the reference line, and the tail of the symbol holds the number 111. The job sheet asks for a 60° included angle, a 1.5 mm root face and a 2.5 mm root gap. Odane has ground the first plate's bevel at about 45° and left a root face of about 4 mm.

c2.title: Setting up the gas set in Port Antonio
c2.text: At a training centre in Port Antonio, Portland, Shanice's group is assembling an oxy-acetylene set for the morning's practical. The acetylene cylinder arrived this morning lying on its side in the back of a pickup and has just been stood up on the trolley. The oxygen regulator's inlet nut has a smear of grease on it from a trainee's hands. One fuel gas hose has a small burnt patch about a metre from the torch. The nozzle chart gives 0.3 bar for both gases.

c3.title: Two jobs for a small shop in Christiana
c3.text: Kemoy works at a small welding shop in Christiana, Manchester. He has two jobs this week: patching a rusted hole in the 1.2 mm sheet steel hopper of a farmer's coffee pulper, and making a base frame of 10 mm plate for a water pump. The shop has a 220 V arc welder, an oxy-acetylene set, E6013 electrodes, copper-coated mild steel filler rods in labelled tubes, and an old bundle of bare rods with no label lying in a corner.

c4.title: A loader bracket on a sugar estate near Frome
c4.text: Tevin is preparing to repair a cracked bracket on a cane loader in a sugar estate workshop near Frome, Westmoreland. The bracket is 25 mm medium-carbon steel. The WPS asks for E7018 electrodes and a preheat of 150 °C, checked 75 mm from the joint. He must also fit a new stiffener of 10 mm plate to the bracket as a tee joint, to be welded on one side only.

c5.title: Setting up the arc bay in Runaway Bay
c5.text: Jodian is setting up an MMAW bay at a training centre in Runaway Bay, St Ann, for the tee-joint practical. She finds the machine standing by the open roller door, in the sun, with rain water pooled under one corner. The work return clamp has been clipped to the machine's case. The insulation on the electrode holder's handle is cracked, with a piece missing near the jaws.

questions.q: What does the number 111 in the tail of Odane's weld symbol tell him?
o: The weld must be 111 mm long on each side
The process is manual metal arc welding
The weld must be made in 1 run, 1 pass, 1 side
The job uses drawing sheet number 111
questions.why: The tail carries extra information such as the process or the WPS. In the ISO numbering of processes, 111 is MMAW and 311 is oxy-acetylene welding.

questions.q: On this AWS drawing the V sits below the reference line. Where must the V preparation be?
o: On the side of the joint the arrow points to
On the side of the joint away from the arrow
On both sides of the joint, as a double-V
On whichever side is easier to reach
questions.why: On AWS drawings a symbol below the reference line means the arrow side; above means the other side. ISO drawings show the other side with a dashed line instead, so always check which system a drawing uses.

questions.q: What bevel angle should Odane grind on each plate to get the 60° included angle?
o: 60° on each plate
45° on each plate
30° on each plate
15° on each plate
questions.why: The included angle is the total of the two bevels, so 30° on each plate gives 60°. His 45° bevels would make a 90° V, needing far more weld metal and heat, and giving more distortion.

questions.q: If Odane welds the joint with the 4 mm root face he has left, what is the most likely fault?
o: The root will burn through and sag below the plate
The weld face will be badly undercut at both toes
The arc will be pushed to one side by magnetism
The root run will not melt right through
questions.why: A root face is there to stop the root burning away, but a thick one cannot be melted through, leaving incomplete root penetration. He should grind it back to an even 1.5 mm as the job sheet says.

questions.q: What should be done about the acetylene cylinder that was carried lying down?
o: Stand it upright for the time the supplier gives before use
Use it at once, as long as it is now chained upright on the trolley
Open its valve fully for a few seconds to clear the acetone out
Lay it back down and use it flat until it is empty
questions.why: Acetylene is dissolved in liquid acetone. A cylinder that has been lying down must stand upright for a while before use, or acetone can be drawn out into the regulator and hoses.

questions.q: What should Shanice do about the grease on the oxygen regulator's inlet nut?
o: Fit it anyway, as a little grease helps the thread to seal
Wipe it with an oily rag so the thread does not rust
Keep it off the cylinder, tag it, and report it for cleaning
Wrap the thread with tape so the grease cannot reach the gas
questions.why: Oil and grease can catch fire or explode when oxygen under pressure reaches them. An oxygen fitting with grease on it is not used until it has been cleaned or replaced by a competent person.

questions.q: What should be done about the fuel gas hose with the burnt patch?
o: Wrap the burnt patch tightly with insulating tape
Use it if a leak test shows no bubbles at that spot
Run it at a lower pressure until a new one comes
Take it out of use and have the hose replaced
questions.why: A burnt hose is weakened and can split or leak at any time, even if it passes a leak test today. Damaged hoses are replaced, never taped or patched.

questions.q: Before the cylinder valves are opened, what should be done to each regulator's adjusting screw?
o: Screw it fully in so the gas can flow at once
Set it to the 0.3 bar the nozzle chart gives
Take it off so the gauges can be read clearly
Wind it out until it turns freely and loosely
questions.why: With the adjusting screw wound out, the regulator is closed, so the full cylinder pressure does not slam into it when the valve opens. The working pressure is set afterwards by turning the screw in.

questions.q: A trainee wants to set the acetylene to 1.5 bar "to get a bigger flame". Why is this wrong?
o: The hose colour shows it is made for low pressure only
Above about 1 bar acetylene can break down and explode
The arrestor will shut off all gas above 1 bar
A higher pressure makes the flame burn too cold
questions.why: Acetylene becomes unstable above about 1 bar (15 psi) and can decompose violently even without air. A bigger flame comes from a bigger nozzle, chosen from the maker's chart.

questions.q: Why is OAW a better choice than MMAW for patching the 1.2 mm hopper?
o: The flame melts the coffee residue off the steel as it welds
Its softer heat is less likely to burn through thin sheet
OAW welds are stronger than arc welds on all kinds of steel
OAW needs no cleaning of the metal before welding
questions.why: Thin sheet burns through easily under a concentrated arc. The gas flame's heat is softer and easier to control, and the filler is added separately, so the welder can manage the pool on thin metal.

questions.q: Why would Kemoy use MMAW, not OAW, for the 10 mm pump base frame?
o: OAW is slow on plate and its wide heat distorts it
OAW cannot melt steel thicker than about 5 mm at all
Gas filler rods are not made thick enough for 10 mm plate
E6013 electrodes are made only for 10 mm plate
questions.why: OAW can weld thick plate, but only slowly, and its wide heat pulls the frame out of shape. The arc's concentrated heat is quicker and gives less distortion on plate of this thickness.

questions.q: What should Kemoy do with the bundle of bare rods that has no label?
o: Use them on the pump frame, where the weld is hidden
Clean the rust off them and use them as filler rods
Set them aside and report them as unidentified
Use them for tacks only and the labelled rods for the welds
questions.why: A rod you cannot identify may be the wrong metal for the job, and the weld could crack or fail. Only use consumables you can identify from their label or packet.

questions.q: Why are the filler rods for gas welding mild steel coated with copper?
o: To make the weld stronger than the plate
To act as a flux and clean the weld pool
To lower the melting point of the rod
To stop the rods rusting in storage
questions.why: The thin copper coat protects the steel rod from rust while it is stored. It does not act as a flux; mild steel gas welding needs no flux.

questions.q: Tevin strokes a 150 °C temperature crayon on the bracket 75 mm from the joint. It leaves a dry, chalky mark. What does this tell him?
o: The bracket is hot enough and welding can start
It is still below 150 °C, so he keeps heating
The bracket is too hot and must cool before welding
The crayon does not work on medium-carbon steel
questions.why: A temperature crayon melts to a glossy liquid when the metal has reached its rated temperature. A dry mark means the metal is still below that temperature.

questions.q: Why should Tevin heat a wide band on both sides of the crack rather than just the crack itself?
o: To burn the paint off the whole bracket at the same time
To save gas, because wide heating takes less time
So the area round the weld cools slowly and evenly
So the crack closes up before he starts to weld
questions.why: Preheat works by slowing the cooling of the weld and the metal beside it. Heating only a spot leaves cold metal close by that draws the heat away fast, which is what causes hardening and cracking.

questions.q: The new 10 mm stiffener will be welded on one side only. How should Tevin pre-set it before tacking?
o: Lean it slightly away from the side that will be welded
Lean it slightly towards the side that will be welded
Set it exactly square, because pre-setting is only for butt joints
Leave a wide gap under it so the weld can pull it down
questions.why: The fillet shrinks as it cools and pulls the upright towards the weld. Leaning it slightly the other way lets the shrinkage pull it back to 90°.

questions.q: After tacking one end of the stiffener, Tevin's square shows it is 3° out. What should he do?
o: Weld it as it is and hammer it straight afterwards
Add a much bigger weld on the far side to pull it back
Leave it, since 3° is too small to matter on a bracket
Grind off the tack, re-square it and tack again
questions.why: It is quick to correct a joint while it is held by one small tack, and very hard once it is fully welded. Extra weld or hammering adds stresses and can crack the medium-carbon steel.

questions.q: Where should Jodian fix the work return clamp?
o: On the machine's case, so the circuit is as short as possible
On the steel leg of the bay's screen, out of the way
On clean metal on the job or the bench, near the joint
On the water pipe beside the bay, which is a good earth
questions.why: The clamp completes the welding circuit through the job, so it goes on clean metal close to the weld. On the machine case, a screen or a pipe, the current takes stray paths that can damage equipment, start fires or give shocks.

questions.q: What should Jodian do about the cracked electrode holder?
o: Tag it DO NOT USE, report it and use a sound holder
Wrap the crack with insulating tape and carry on
Use it but wear two pairs of gloves for extra cover
Use it only for tacking, as tacks need little current
questions.why: Cracked or missing insulation can expose live metal and give a shock. A damaged holder is taken out of use, tagged so nobody else picks it up, and reported for repair or replacement.

questions.q: Where should the welding machine stand?
o: Where it is now, as the roller door gives it plenty of fresh air
On a dry, level floor in the shade, with space round its vents
Inside a closed cupboard, safe from dust and the rain
On a wooden pallet in the doorway, raised above the water
questions.why: Water near a machine raises the risk of shock, and sun and blocked vents make it overheat sooner. A dry, level, shaded spot with air round the vents keeps it safe and cool.
